answer:
**Normalization methods differ mainly in which values share statistics.** BatchNorm pools batch and spatial observations for each channel. LayerNorm typically normalizes features within one example/token. InstanceNorm normalizes each image/channel across spatial positions. GroupNorm normalizes groups of channels and spatial positions within each example. [1](https://arxiv.org/abs/1502.03167)

**Why the axes matter.** With two images of different brightness, BatchNorm uses their shared batch statistics, while InstanceNorm treats each image independently. LayerNorm in a language model does not need another user's tokens to normalize the current token. The same mean/variance formula applied over different axes creates different information dependencies.

Small batches make BatchNorm's estimates noisy, and training/inference statistics may differ. A batch size of one is not automatically impossible for every convolutional BatchNorm because spatial positions also contribute observations; the truly degenerate case has only one value in a normalized channel. The broader issue is estimate quality and coupling to batch composition.

Autoregressive inference also favors per-token normalization: the model often processes one new token and should not depend on unavailable future tokens or arbitrary concurrent requests. GroupNorm is useful in some small-batch vision settings because it avoids batch statistics.

Choose based on architecture, task, and serving conditions. Test train/eval behavior, batch-size changes, and the exact normalized axes instead of assuming all norms are interchangeable stabilization layers.

**Technical details and references.**

For NCHW images, BatchNorm computes statistics per channel across batch and spatial axes; InstanceNorm uses spatial axes per sample/channel; GroupNorm uses spatial axes and a channel group per sample. LayerNorm normalizes a chosen feature shape per example or token. [1](https://arxiv.org/abs/1502.03167) [4](https://docs.pytorch.org/docs/stable/index.html)

$$\hat x=(x-\mu)/\sqrt{\sigma^2+\epsilon},\qquad y=\gamma\hat x+\beta.$$

Small batches make BN estimates noisy, but batch size one is not automatically invalid if there are many spatial observations. A channel with only one training value cannot supply meaningful variance. Autoregressive models need consistent per-token behavior and must avoid leaking future positions through statistics. LN/RMSNorm avoid dependence on other examples; GN offers a batch-independent alternative for vision. Check train/eval running-stat behavior explicitly.
